Probably not. The S&P 500 index fund is a fine holding, but 100% in it at 56 is the problem, not the "single fund" part.

The main risk is sequence-of-returns: a large drop in the years just before or after you start withdrawing does permanent damage because you're selling shares at low prices. The S&P 500 fell about 50% in 2000-02 and about 55% in 2007-09, and 2000-2009 as a whole had a negative total return. With roughly 10 years to retirement, you may not have time to recover from a drop like that. The fund is also US-only and top-heavy, with its largest handful of stocks making up a large share of the index, so it is less diversified than it looks.

The case for it is real. Retirement may last 30+ years, so you need growth, and an all-equity portfolio has historically won over long horizons. It's defensible if guaranteed income (pension, Social Security, an annuity) covers your essential expenses, or if you hold a separate bond or cash reserve outside this account. It also makes more sense if you could work longer or cut spending in a downturn, and if you would not sell in a 40% drop. That last condition is the one people most often overestimate.

For comparison, target-date funds for your retirement year typically hold roughly 55-75% stocks, with the rest in bonds. A single target-date fund gives you one-fund simplicity with a built-in glide path.

Two things would change this answer: how much of your spending is covered by guaranteed income, and whether this money is in a tax-advantaged account. If it's taxable, selling your current holdings to switch could trigger capital gains tax.
